parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Start by picturing the hydrogen protons in the body with no field applied - their tiny nuclear magnetic moments point in random directions. What must a magnetic field do to create some order?
Hint 2: Remember that once aligned, protons can sit in a lower or an upper energy state and precess. Why does the field need to be both constant and very large for a clear, detectable signal?
parts.proper_answer: The large constant field aligns the magnetic moments of hydrogen protons and splits them into two energy states. The majority occupy the lower energy state and precess at the Larmor frequency, allowing resonant excitation by a radio-frequency pulse.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Create alignment from randomness**
Think of each hydrogen nucleus (a proton) as a tiny spinning magnet. Normally they point every which way so there is no net magnetism. When you apply a strong uniform $B$ field, these spins line up either parallel or anti-parallel to the field, just like compass needles.

Step 2: **Make two energy levels and precession**
The two alignments have slightly different energies. A few more protons sit in the lower energy state, giving a net magnetisation. The protons also precess about the field direction at the Larmor frequency. A large $B$ gives a large energy split and a high, well-defined precession frequency, so a short radio-frequency pulse can excite resonance and be detected on relaxation.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Imagine the whole body was in exactly the same field, so every proton precessed and emitted at exactly the same frequency. Could you tell which part of the body the signal came from?
Hint 2: Recall that precession frequency is directly proportional to the magnetic flux density at that point. What happens to the frequency if $B$ is made to vary smoothly with position?
parts.proper_answer: The non-uniform (gradient) field is superimposed so that the total magnetic field varies with position. Hence the Larmor frequency varies with position, so the frequency of the detected radio signal identifies where in the body it originated, enabling an image to be formed.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **The problem with a uniform field alone**
With only the large constant field, all protons in the body precess at the same Larmor frequency and emit the same frequency on de-excitation. You would detect a signal but have no idea whether it came from the left, right, top or bottom.

Step 2: **Encode position in frequency**
Adding a small gradient field makes the total $B$ field slightly bigger at one side than the other. Since Larmor frequency $f$ is proportional to $B$, $f$ now depends on position. By measuring the exact frequency of the emitted radio wave, the scanner can work out the position of those protons. Scanning the gradient in different directions builds up a full 3D map.
